either-error-handling
Either (Error Handling)
Better than Option for errors (holds error or value):
def divide(a: Int, b: Int): Either[String, Int] = {
  if (b == 0) Left("Cannot divide by zero")
  else Right(a / b)
}

divide(10, 2) match {
  case Right(result) => println(s"Result: $result")
  case Left(error) => println(s"Error: $error")
}

// Combinators
divide(10, 2).map(_ * 2)              // Right(10)
divide(10, 0).map(_ * 2)              // Left("Cannot divide by zero")

divide(10, 2).fold(
  err => println(s"Failed: $err"),
  result => println(s"Got: $result")
)

tips-tricks
💡 Tips & Tricks
Use pattern matching over instanceof
: Scala's pattern matching is type-safe, exhaustiveness-checked, and cleaner than Java's casting.
For comprehensions for sequential operations
: Especially with 
/
Either
, they're cleaner than manual 
.flatMap()
for {
  x <- Some(1)
  y <- Some(2)
  z <- Some(3)
} yield x + y + z          // Some(6)

// vs
Some(1).flatMap(x => Some(2).flatMap(y => Some(3).map(z => x + y + z)))
  x <- Some(1)
  y <- Some(2)
  z <- Some(3)
} yield x + y + z          // Some(6)
// vs
Some(1).flatMap(x => Some(2).flatMap(y => Some(3).map(z => x + y + z)))
Use 
 / 
dropWhile
 instead of break
: These functional alternatives are cleaner and composable.
(1 to 100).takeWhile(_ < 50)    // stops at first false
(1 to 100).dropWhile(_ < 50)    // skips while condition is true
(1 to 100).takeWhile(_ < 50)    // stops at first false
(1 to 100).dropWhile(_ < 50)    // skips while condition is true
Match with guards for complex conditions
: More readable than nested ifs.
x match {
  case n if n < 0 => "negative"
  case n if n == 0 => "zero"
  case n if n > 0 => "positive"
}
  case n if n < 0 => "negative"
  case n if n == 0 => "zero"
  case n if n > 0 => "positive"
️-edge-cases-gotchas
⚠️ Edge Cases & Gotchas
Pattern matching must be exhaustive
: Missing a case causes a compile warning (or error with 
-Werror
). Always use 
case _ =>
 for unknown cases.
Option/Either require pattern matching or combinators
: You can't just call 
.value
; use 
.getOrElse()
 or pattern match.
val x: Option[Int] = Some(5)
x.value                           // compile error
x.getOrElse(0)                    // 5
val x: Option[Int] = Some(5)
x.value                           // compile error
x.getOrElse(0)                    // 5
Try is not the same as Option
Try[T]
 holds a value or a 
Throwable
. Similar API but different semantics.
import scala.util.Try
Try(10 / 0)                       // Failure(ArithmeticException)
Try(10 / 2)                       // Success(5)
import scala.util.Try
Try(10 / 0)                       // Failure(ArithmeticException)
Try(10 / 2)                       // Success(5)
for
 loops don't return values; use 
for (... yield ...)
 for that
for (x <- 1 to 5) println(x)      // Unit (side effect)
val result = for (x <- 1 to 5) yield x * 2  // Vector(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
for (x <- 1 to 5) println(x)      // Unit (side effect)
val result = for (x <- 1 to 5) yield x * 2  // Vector(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
Variable scoping in for loops
: Loop variables are local to the loop.
for (i <- 1 to 5) println(i)
println(i)                        // compile error (i out of scope)
for (i <- 1 to 5) println(i)
println(i)                        // compile error (i out of scope)
Guard conditions in pattern matching can have side effects
: Use with caution.
x match {
  case n if { println(s"Checking $n"); n > 0 } => "positive"
  case _ => "other"
}
  case n if { println(s"Checking $n"); n > 0 } => "positive"
